title: Which numbers are independence roots? Polynomial divisors, well-covered graphs and imaginary roots of large modulus
shortTitle: Exactly which numbers are independence roots
oneLine: A number is a zero of some graph's independence polynomial exactly when its reciprocal is an algebraic integer and no conjugate is positive real; i times the golden ratio is one, on a 4,293-vertex graph.
abstract: The independence polynomial of a graph counts its independent vertex sets (sets with no edges between them) by size; in statistical physics it is the partition function of the hard-core lattice gas, and its complex zeros are called independence roots. Two restrictions on independence roots are immediate: the reciprocal of a root is an algebraic integer, and no root or algebraic conjugate of a root is a positive real number. Roots are known to be dense in the plane, but density does not say which numbers are hit exactly. This candidate proves that the two restrictions are the only ones: a nonzero complex number is an independence root if and only if its reciprocal is an algebraic integer and none of its conjugates is positive real. Equivalently, an integer polynomial with constant term one divides some independence polynomial exactly when it is positive on the nonnegative real axis, and connected cographs, trees and connected well-covered graphs each realise every such divisor. The criterion describes every purely imaginary independence root and answers Cameron's question on purely imaginary roots of modulus greater than one: they exist, for example i times the golden ratio on an explicit graph with 4,293 vertices. Such roots first appear at independence number six, where they are dense on the imaginary axis; a number whose conjugates are all purely imaginary needs independence number exactly its degree plus two. At independence number six the largest purely imaginary root of an N-vertex graph has modulus asymptotic to 6^(−9/10)·3^(−3/4)·N^(2/5), with a power-saving error term. Limits: the witnesses are large and the minimal one is unknown; the sharp size law covers only independence number six; the tree construction can add roots. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 2.1 and Corollary 2.2 (proof, main): an integer polynomial f with f(0) = 1 divides some independence polynomial iff f > 0 on [0, ∞); a nonzero z is an independence root iff 1/z is an algebraic integer and no conjugate of z is positive real. Connected cographs, trees and connected well-covered graphs each realise every such divisor, with multiplicities kept for cographs and well-covered graphs.

Section 4 (explicit construction, exactly verified): i·(1+√5)/2 is an independence root of a 4,293-vertex graph with independence number six, I_G = (1+3x²+x⁴)(1+4293x+2430x²); this answers Cameron's question on purely imaginary roots of modulus greater than one.

Theorem 4.2 and Corollary 4.3 (proof): a number of degree d whose conjugates are all purely imaginary needs independence number exactly d+2; six is the least independence number with a purely imaginary root of modulus above one, and at six such roots are dense on the imaginary axis.

Theorem 5.1 and Theorem A.2 (proof): at independence number six the largest purely imaginary root of an N-vertex graph has modulus 6^(−9/10)·3^(−3/4)·N^(2/5)·(1 + O(N^(−1/15))); in arbitrary directions the growth is N^5.

Theorem 6.1 and Corollary 7.1 (proof): every integral ray in the interior of the Cutler–Pebody cone is realised exactly by well-covered graphs; z is a root of a well-covered tree iff 1/z is an algebraic integer and every real conjugate lies in [−1, 0).

narration:
This is an audio briefing from Evidence Press on a research candidate about networks and the numbers hidden in their quiet groups.

Take any network. An independent set is a group of nodes with no links between them, like guests at a party none of whom know each other. Count these groups by size and use the counts as the coefficients of a polynomial, the independence polynomial. Physicists know it as the partition function of the hard-core gas, where its complex zeros mark possible phase transitions.

Which complex numbers can be zeros of such a polynomial, for some network? Two restrictions are obvious. The reciprocal of a zero must be an algebraic integer, and no zero, nor any of its algebraic twins, can be a positive real number, because the polynomial is positive there. Earlier work showed that zeros come arbitrarily close to every point, but not which points are hit exactly.

This candidate shows that the obvious restrictions are the only ones. Every number that passes them is a zero, and the network can be chosen to be a tree, a cograph or a well-covered graph.

It also settles a question about zeros on the imaginary axis. Such zeros can be larger than one in size: the imaginary unit times the golden ratio is a zero of an explicit network with four thousand two hundred and ninety-three nodes. These large imaginary zeros need groups of at least six nodes, and once six is allowed they come as close as you like to every point of the axis.

The constructions join together clusters of fully linked nodes, whose group counts can be tuned exactly, and a classical counting inequality bounds how large the zeros can get.

There are limits. The networks are huge, the smallest one with the golden-ratio zero is unknown, and the sharp size law is proved only when the largest group has six nodes.

This is an unrefereed candidate, checked by internal AI-assisted review and exact computation rather than by peer review, and this briefing uses a synthetic voice that is not additional evidence.

relatedWorks.citation: Ball, Galvin, Hyry and Weingartner (2022), Independent set and matching permutations. Journal of Graph Theory. Exact top-down correction of independent-set counts in joins of disjoint cliques, a source of the gadgets used here.
Bencs (2018), On trees with real-rooted independence polynomial. Discrete Mathematics. Proposition 2.7: the stable-path tree of a connected graph, used to transfer roots to trees.

Brown and Cameron (2020), A note on purely imaginary independence roots. Discrete Mathematics. Roots ±i/k, no imaginary roots at independence number at most three, and the questions on smallest order and irrational multiples of i.
Brown and Cameron (2020), Maximum modulus of independence roots of graphs and trees. Graphs and Combinatorics. The maximum modulus when the independence number is free.

Brown, Dilcher and Nowakowski (2000), Roots of independence polynomials of well covered graphs. Journal of Algebraic Combinatorics. Roots of a well-covered graph have modulus at most its independence number.

Brown, Hickman and Nowakowski (2004), On the location of roots of independence polynomials. Journal of Algebraic Combinatorics. Independence roots are dense in the complex plane, also for well-covered graphs.

Cutler and Pebody (2017), Maximal-clique partitions and the Roller Coaster Conjecture. Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A. Approximate realisation of well-covered counting vectors, made exact in Section 6.
Dubickas (2007), On roots of polynomials with positive coefficients. Manuscripta Mathematica. The analogue for positive rational coefficients, settling a conjecture of Kuba.
Fisher and Ryan (1992), Bounds on the number of complete subgraphs. Discrete Mathematics. The clique-count inequality behind the sharp size law.
Fox (2011), A new proof of the graph removal lemma. Annals of Mathematics. The removal lemma used in Section 5.

Jerrum and Patel (2026), Zero-free regions for the independence polynomial on restricted graph classes. Journal of the London Mathematical Society. Zero-free regions for bounded-degree classes, in contrast with the unbounded-degree witnesses here.
Levit and Mandrescu (2008), On the roots of independence polynomials of almost all very well-covered graphs. Discrete Applied Mathematics. Background on well-covered trees used in Section 7.

Ma and Zhang (2026), Extending Brown and Cameron's classification of purely imaginary independence roots. Zenodo. Concurrent work: i times b is a root for rational b squared exactly when b squared is 1/k.
Motzkin and Straus (1969), Divisors of polynomials and power series with positive coefficients. Pacific Journal of Mathematics. The classical positivity multiplier used in Lemma 3.2.
